name: I Crossed Into Canada
author: Vasile Korhonen-Adeyemi, freelance courier
description:
I crossed into Canada at the Port Huron checkpoint on a Tuesday in November. I had my papers in order — GLMZ transit visa, GLMZ work registration, medical clearance. I'd heard the border was efficient. I was not prepared for what efficient meant.

The checkpoint is a corridor. Clean white surfaces, ambient lighting that adjusts as you walk — warmer ahead, cooler behind, guiding you forward without signage. I didn't see a single sign in the entire facility. I didn't need one. The architecture itself communicated. A soft chime indicated where to stop. A panel illuminated where I should place my documents. A voice — warm, feminine, speaking English with a faint Ottawa Valley inflection that I'm certain was a deliberate design choice — welcomed me to Canada and asked the purpose of my visit. I said business. The voice said 'Wonderful' and meant nothing by it.

The biometric scan took four seconds. The document verification took two. My visa was approved, stamped with a holographic maple leaf, and returned to me through a slot that opened exactly where my hand was already resting. The timing was unsettling. The system knew where my hand would be before I did. A second voice — male, equally warm, equally empty — wished me a pleasant stay in Canada and reminded me that my visa permitted ninety days of residency with access to all public services including healthcare, transit, and emergency assistance.

I walked through the exit corridor and into Canada. The air was clean. The road was perfect — no cracks, no patches, no wear. A transit vehicle was waiting at the curb, already programmed with my declared destination. I hadn't told anyone my destination. I'd listed it on my visa application eleven days earlier. The vehicle's interior was comfortable, climate-controlled, and silent. A screen displayed a welcome message in English and French. The message included my name.

I sat in the vehicle for forty-five minutes as it drove me through countryside that looked maintained but uninhabited. The fields were tended. The roads were clear. The buildings I passed had lights on but no movement visible through the windows. I arrived at my destination, completed my business, and returned to the border three days later. The exit process was identical in its perfection. A voice thanked me for visiting Canada. I did not feel thanked. I felt catalogued.

story_hooks: How did the border system predict the exact position of the courier's hand?
What business required a personal visit to automated Canada?
